rows.text: The hams gave off a faint, salty smell. Curing had done wonders for the meat, though Mortimer’s disposition evidently required a different process.
A ham turned slightly beneath the awning, presenting its better side. Death had done little to cure its vanity.
Steam warmed the air around Gerald, who remained personally unthawed. The machine endured considerable pressure, though nothing compared with being expected to produce coffee worthy of him.
The machine gave a thin, superior hiss. Gerald had warmed to you, but the coffee still considered itself out of your league.
The light in the crack twitched, suggesting the fountain had received another rumour. Unlike water, these could circulate indefinitely without ever becoming clear.
The light briefly brightened, lending the fountain an air of credibility. This was how rumours became history, provided nobody checked whether the plumbing worked.
Portia gave a small, stony creak. It was impressive how much refusal could be fitted into a structure whose entire purpose was to let people through.
The archway gave off a faint smell of hot stone. Winning its affection had apparently been easier than persuading it that a name was not a structural commitment.
Light caught on a book’s spine and was made to feel it was browsing without buying. Marginalia remained unimpressed, a difficult distinction to maintain in a room full of professionally closed minds.
The air between the books was cool with the confidence of stock that had no intention of moving. Selling was tolerated here, but only as a lapse in judgment.
The roots smelled faintly of dry wood, which was reassuring; at least something here was decaying in the usual direction.
A root of the dead branch twitched toward the light, displaying the sort of optimism usually confined to fresh produce priced to sell tomorrow.
